              POST-HEARING REPLY BRIEF OF MEYER E11 INTERVENORS

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

           COMES NOW Paul & Jane Meyer Family Foundation, SM Retreat Ltd. and Leslie Meyer

Rhea [“Meyer E11 Intervenors”], and pursuant to SOAH Orders No. 6 and 32 file this Post-

Hearing Reply Brief of Meyer E11 Intervenors in the above-entitled docket:

      I.          Unchanged Statement of Position

           The Meyer E11 Intervenors are not advocating for any particular route. The Meyer E11

Intervenors, as would be expected, are opposed to any route that includes links E6, E7, E8, E11

and E12. In short, we are opposed to any route that cuts through the City of Belton and the north

side of Salado, i.e. the northern routes in the eastern half of the study area.

     II.          Minimal Briefing Insisting on Route 392

           Of all the intervenors in this case and the many initial briefs filed, there are only two

intervenor groups arguing that the only choice for the ALJs and Commissioners is Route 392. The

primary advocacy comes from the two initial briefs filed by the aligned Brady Creek/Solana

                                                                                              Page 1
 intervenor group. Interchange 6280 and 6282. The Mewhinney Family also briefed their support

of the Brady Creek arguments. Interchange 6224. As will be discussed below, other intervenors

advocated in general for “northern routes” that included options superior to Route 392.

       The Brady Creek/Solana briefing, over the course of almost seventy cumulative pages,

boils down to three basic arguments that are simply repeated over and over. First they argue that

the Colorado River crossing is the only portion of the study area that really matters in the routing

decision. Second they contend that existing transmission lines and roads are the only forms of

compatible right-of-way that should be counted. The third contention is that cost and habitable

structures are the only advantages to Route 894 and should be discounted because Mr. Wulff, Jr.

speculates that the cost estimates might be questionable. The Brady Creek/Solana briefing

amounts to route analysis by exclusion rather than the holistic approach required by PURA and

Commission rules.

    III.       ALJs Must Choose a Route, Not a Single River Crossing

       Contrary to the myopic argument the extreme position of Brady Creek/Solana and their

supporters require, the obligation of the ALJs is undeniable. As set out in PURA, the PUC rules

and the Commission’s Order of Referral, the ALJs are required to recommend a complete route

based on an analysis of all factors as applied to the entire length of the route. It would be an

absolute violation of PURA to base a routing decision for a 220+ mile long route on the sole factor

of environmental impact of a single river crossing – no matter how significant the river.

       Still, the Brady Creek/Solana approach is clear. Their briefs argue that the Colorado River

crossing is the only feature in the Study Area that differentiates the routes. The residents in and

around Belton and Salado of course contend that a major differentiator would be municipal city

limits and residential neighborhoods. The intervenors naturally have competing ideas of what



                                                                                              Page 2
 portion of the Study Area and issue is the most important. That is precisely why PURA requires

a route-level analysis balancing all the enumerated factors. Some study areas may necessitate

greater importance to some factors over others, but there is no study area that is so unique that the

analysis should be limited to a single river crossing.

       The Brady Creek/Solana argument brings to mind the parable of the three blind men asked

to describe an elephant. One feels the trunk, the second the body, and the third the tail. They

describe completely different animals. Brady Creek/Solana asks the ALJs and Commissioners to

put on blinders and only examine a very narrow point in the Study Area. PURA requires that the

entire elephant be examined and that a route – not a crossing – be recommended.

       If the Joint Applicants truly provided links and routes that only allowed for one rational

choice for crossing the Colorado River, the proper resolution would be to grant a challenge to route

adequacy and force the Applicants to provide more and better options. As pointed out by the Brady

Creek/Solana Intervenors more than once, the Joint Applicants concluded that every link and route

in the Application is both constructable and viable – including all the links crossing the Colorado

River. The route adequacy challenge in this docket was denied, and the PUC Commissioners voted

unanimously to deny the appeal of that decision. The proposed routes have been found to provide

adequate choices, including at the Colorado River crossing. All links crossing the Colorado River

are viable and up for consideration.

    IV.         All Compatible Rights-of-Way Count

          The next key to the Brady Creek/Solana argument is that the ALJs and Commissioners

should ignore half of the compatible right-of-way metrics and only focus on existing transmission

lines and roads. There is no legal basis for this argument. PURA and the PUC rules clearly include

apparent property boundaries, railroads and pipelines.



                                                                                               Page 3
         Even though the community expressed specific concerns about property fragmentation at

the open houses, as was discussed in our Initial Brief, Brady Creek/Solana contends that this

measurable factor should be disregarded based solely on their unsupported conjecture that their

properties are more likely than others to be bisected or made up of multiple tax assessment tracts.

The vast majority of the direct testimony filed in this case describes how each landowners’

property will be bisected by the proposed links. Even a casual glance at the Intervenor Maps

prepared by the Joint Applicants confirm that all the Meyer E11 tracts would be bisected, as would

most of the intervenors on Links E6, E7, E8, E11 and E12. Joint Applicants’ Exhibits 20 and 21.

Property fragmentation is not unique to the Colorado River crossings, nor is the conjecture about

tax parcels making the data in the Environmental Assessment unreliable. If evidence had been

presented with a superior review of property boundary data for every link in the Study Area, the

ALJs and Commissioners might choose to consider it. However, there is no justification for

ignoring all the existing data in the record based on assumptions made regarding a single link.

        Inexplicably, the Brady Creek brief completely ignores the pipeline right-of-way

paralleling. The obvious explanation is that Route 392 has zero pipeline right-of-way, while

Routes 894 and 487 parallel over two miles each. The Solana brief contends that pipeline

paralleling is “no longer a preferred routing characteristic” and should instead be used to exclude

routes. Regardless of the preferences of their paid expert, pipeline right-of-way is still a factor that

measured in every environmental assessment and should be included in the route analysis. It is

disingenuous for intervenors to exclude the half of the right-of-way data unfavorable to their

argument and then claim that their preferred route is superior. All compatible right-of-way needs

to be evaluated, because the ALJs and Commissioners are not legally permitted to simply ignore

factors and their related data.



                                                                                                  Page 4
        As discussed in our Initial Brief, when all forms of compatible right-of-way are examined

together, Routes 894 and 487 perform better than the minority route pushed by Brady

Creek/Solana.

     V.          It’s Not All About Cost and Habs

       The Brady Creek/Solana briefs make the spurious argument that the only reason to select

Route 894 is because of cost and habitable structure counts. As was demonstrated in our Initial

Brief, there are at least eleven routing factors other than cost, length and habitable structures in

which Routes 894 and 487 and dramatically superior to Route 392:

     1)          Total length paralleling compatible ROW (19.5% less)
     2)          Crossing potential wetlands (22.8% more)
     3)          Stream crossings (14.9% more)
     4)          Recorded cultural resource sites crossed (8 times as many)
     5)          Cultural resource sites w/in 1,000 feet (almost 3 times as many)
     6)          Length over high archeological/historical potential (28.4% more)
     7)          FAA-registered airports (50% more)
     8)          FM/microwave installations (more than twice as many)
     9)          Highway crossings (16 2/3% more)
    10)          FM/County road crossings (55.3% more)
    11)          Foreground visual zone of highways (88% more)


The “Northern Corridor” route is also the only one of the three that crosses any upland woodland

areas, parallels streams, or is near heliports and AM transmitters. Joint Applicants’ Exhibit 23

(Route by Miles tab).

          The Brady Creek/Solana intervenors and the few others favorable to Route 392 would have

the ALJs and Commissioners not only limit their review to the single crossing of the Colorado

River, but also to the small subset of environmental factors of riparian land crossing and viewshed.

There are a dozen other factors that support either Route 894 or Route 487 (and many others) as

far superior choices to the minority route.




                                                                                              Page 5
     VI.        Viewshed Is Universal

       The Brady Creek brief devotes multiple pages in various sections to the issue of viewshed

and the viewshed study prepared by the Staten Creek Intervenors. Like the property fragmentation

issue, this is not something unique to the Colorado River crossings. Through testimony and

photographs, the Brady Creek Intervenors argue that “the Applicants' HVTL towers of Route 894

would dominate the landscape.” Brady Creek Brief, p. 15. The 200-foot clear-cut right-of-way

and almost 200-foot towers will “dominate the landscape” on every potential link in the Study

Area. Virtually every direct testimony filed by a landowner in this docket says the same thing

about the visual impact of such towers and right-of-way on their property. The Meyer E11

Intervenors describe how not just the appearance but the noise of the lines would fundamentally

change the natural, contemplative atmosphere they have created which is essential to the mission

of the SM Retreat. The views around the river crossing will not be impacted to any greater extent

than anywhere else in the Study Area, and the existing views – while admittedly beautiful – are

not substantially more beautiful than views to be found on other links.

       In the Environmental Assessment, the Joint Applicants address the particular concerns for

views from parks and recreational facilities. Joint Applicants’ Exhibit 1, pp. 247-250. Again, as

pointed out by the Brady Creek/Solana Intervenors more than once, the Joint Applicants concluded

that every link and route in the Application is both constructable and viable – including all the

links near parks and recreational areas. This includes parks in the Eastern counties of the Study

Area, not just along the Colorado River.




                                                                                           Page 6
      VII.          Better Routes Including Link U3

         Even if the ALJs and/or Commissioners are convinced by the Brady Creek/Solana

argument that the only acceptable crossing of the Colorado River is U3 and no route containing

another crossing should be considered, there are still better routes to select than 392.

            The 4K Land and Cattle Company brief and the testimony of J. Luther King, Jr. advocates

generally for a “Northern Corridor” route to be selected, but identifies a total of ten routes that

would be acceptable to them – including Route 410. 4K Brief, p. 5. The R1 Opposition Intervenors

advocate for Routes 410 and 894-Western Mod 1 in addition to 392. R1 Brief, pp. 19-21. The

Staten Creek Intervenors also include Route 410 in their recommendation. Staten Creek Brief, p.

6.

        Using a holistic, route-level analysis under PURA, both Routes 410 and 894 Western Mod

1, advocated by other Colorado River area intervenors critical of Route 894, perform significantly

better than Route 392. Comparing the three routes in a manner similar to our Initial Brief analysis

copied above, we see that the Brady Creek/Solana insistence on 392 as the only route results in

not only higher cost and length than Route 894 Western Mod 1, but 392 is also inferior on:

             1)    Habitable structures (70% more than 894WMod1 and 38.7% more than 410)
             2)    Total length paralleling compatible ROW (3% less than 410)
             3)    Length paralleling transmission line ROW (12.4% less than 410)
             4)    Length crossing riparian areas (8% more than 410 and 14.6% more than
                   894WMod1)
             5)    Crossing potential wetlands (23.5% more than 894WMod1)
             6)    Stream crossings (2.9% more than 410 and 5.2% more than 894WMod1)
             7)    Recorded cultural resource sites crossed (8 times as many as 894WMod1)
             8)    Cultural resource sites w/in 1,000 feet (almost 1.48 times as many as 894WMod1)
             9)    Length over high archeological/historical potential (1% more than 410 and 25.25%
                   more than 894WMod1)
            10)    FAA-registered airports (28.6% more than 894WMod1)
            11)    FM/microwave installations (37.5% more than 410 and over twice as many as
                   894WMod1)
            12)    Highway crossings (16 2/3% more than 894WMod1)
            13)    FM/County road crossings (62.2% more than 894WMod1)


                                                                                             Page 7
           14)    Foreground visual zone of highways (3.3% more than 410 and 82% more than
                 894WMod1

In addition, Route 894 Western Mod 1 does not have any ROW in the foreground visual zone of a

park or recreational area.

          As can be seen, the difference in habitable structures impacted is as dramatically higher for

392 than either Route 410 or 894 Western Mod 1. Even if the analysis is narrowed severely to the

highlighted factors preferred by Brady Creek/Solana – paralleling transmission ROW and crossing

riparian areas – their minority choice of 392 is inferior to Route 410, which parallels more

transmission line ROW than 392 and has less length crossing riparian areas. Even by their own

tremendously restrictive analysis, and accepting their assumption that the only viable crossing of

the Colorado River is Link U3, the proper route choice is Route 410, not 392.

  VIII.          Conclusion

       The required holistic review of the routing factors set forth in PURA and the PUC rules

still support either the Joint Applicants’ selection of Route 894 or PUC Staff’s recommendation

of Route 487 based on the entirety of the evidentiary record so painstakingly developed. By

contrast, the Brady Creek/Solana Intervenors, almost alone, advocate for a different approach.

Their analysis begins and ends with the Colorado River crossing. That would make for a very

short transmission line (and a much shorter hearing than was held). The actual Study Area is over

220 miles long. The statute and the Commission’s Order of Referral require that a complete route

be chosen and not a single crossing. They require an end-to-end route-level analysis of all the

routing factors in PURA and the PUC rules. You simply must examine the entire elephant. Even

if the ALJs are somehow persuaded that the Colorado River crossing is the only decision that

matters in this case, and that the only acceptable crossing of the Colorado River is Link U3, Route

410 is a superior route to 392 after reviewing the PURA factors and the record. The Meyer E11


                                                                                                 Page 8
 Intervenors ask that after due consideration of the evidentiary record and all the routing factors the

judges select a route that does not include Links E6, E7, E8, E11 and E12.
